results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec
Every outliner summary matches the controlling idea of the spec paragraph it is aligned to, in spec order (p01-p70); callouts are unaligned front matter.

results.quote: It is not legal advice, and it does not replace counsel; national transposition, guidance and case law change the details.
results.finding: The outliner needed two phrases (scope and disclaimer / claim that a few components beat per-law projects). The draft follows p02, whose controlling idea itself joins the chapter's scope, its limits and its claim, so the split lies in the spec.
Concepts ¶4 (marked two_ideas): the draft frames both phrases as one two-part working rule ('The second part of the rule'), matching p12's single controlling idea; not a second topic.

results.quote: Read together, they ask for three disclosure surfaces; P2B and Omnibus rules then reach seller tooling, price badges and reviews.
results.finding: The outliner needed two phrases. p29's controlling idea is only that four sources ask for three disclosure surfaces; the added preview clause about seller tooling, badges and reviews is a second idea (both flow readers also stumbled here).

results.quote: In November 2025 the Commission proposed repealing the P2B Regulation, citing its overlap with the DSA and the Digital Markets Act, and says its ranking guidelines would remain in application
results.finding: The outliner needed two phrases (P2B notice periods / the repeal proposal). p32 subordinates the repeal ('does not remove the need for the capability'), but the draft gives the repeal news two full sentences with a citation, so it reads as a second topic (flow reader B: a side trip).

Every unit ties to a supporting claim: scene and concepts to S1, DSA to S2, transparency and vertical rules to S3, GDPR to S4, DAC7 and INFORM to S5/S1, compliance, trade-offs, failure modes, CA view and questions to S6, conclusion to the Part V synthesis.

Each table is framed by a sentence stating what it shows (roles table by Concepts ¶3, DSA table by ¶2, DAC7 table by ¶4, trade-off and vertical tables by their lead sentences, components table by Compliance ¶1); figures carry explanatory captions; the INFERENCE callout states its point; quotations from legal texts are followed by what they require of the system. No reader reported unexplained evidence.

results.quote: Four overlapping sources, five rules in all, regulate how a marketplace orders and labels what users see.
results.finding: The declared additional_support transition should carry over DSA Arts. 26 and 27 (ad labels and recommender parameters) from the article table; the opening names neither the DSA nor those articles, so the link to the previous section is left to the reader (flow reader B: 'the section itself never says why it comes next').

All other boundaries express the declared relationship and pick up the declared known information (e.g. 'Ingrid's second question begins with roles', 'Disclosure rules say what to show; GDPR says what to keep', 'DAC7 is the directive behind the reporting-platform-operator role', 'Horizontal rules govern the marketplace', 'Preventing those failures is the Chief Architect's work', 'Part V opened with a test').

results.draft_locus: The Digital Services Act as a Set of System Requirements ¶11
results.quote: Had the November 2027 pipeline existed then, the decision record would carry
results.finding: Both readers had to stop to line up February 2027, March 2027, November 2027 and February 2028 against a narrator who speaks 'as of October 2026'; the timeline is never stated once, so the counterfactual worked example forces a re-read. Flow reader A: 'I had to stop to work out when "now" is.' The spec's order is fine; the prose does not set the timeline.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 4 ('The counterfactual about time made me check the dates')

results.draft_locus: The Digital Services Act as a Set of System Requirements ¶13
results.quote: Veldmark's report for 2027, published in February 2028, was the first produced this way
results.finding: The shared platform 'went live for Tradeyard Netherlands and Belgium in November 2027' (Scene ¶3), yet a full-year, three-platform 2027 report is said to come from its event log; the draft does not explain how. Flow reader A: 'It is not explained how a full-year, three-platform 2027 report came from that event log.'
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 5 ('I paused over how a full-year 2027 report, covering all three platforms, could come from events captured by a platform that started in November for two countries')

results.draft_locus: Concepts: Who Is the Marketplace in Law? ¶3
results.quote: through its definition of "platform", DAC7, which excludes software that "exclusively" allows users "to list or advertise" a relevant activity or processes payments without further intervention
results.finding: The paragraph packs three laws, two quotations and the DAC7 exclusion into two long sentences, and frames DAC7 as turning on a contract although the DAC7 section frames it as handling the money and repeats the exclusion. Flow reader A: 'I re-read it to sort which rules fall on which side.'
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 2 ('the DAC7 part of this sentence needed a second reading ... The point is made twice, framed differently each time')

results.quote: Four overlapping sources, five rules in all, regulate how a marketplace orders and labels what users see. Read together, they ask for three disclosure surfaces; P2B and Omnibus rules then reach seller tooling, price badges and reviews.
results.finding: Three counts in two sentences plus a preview folded after a semicolon. Flow reader A: 'The counts (four, five, three) and the preview clause after the semicolon took a second reading to match against the table.'
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 6 ('Three numbers in two sentences, plus a roadmap folded into a clause after a semicolon')

results.draft_locus: Beyond the EU: UK and US Rules in Brief ¶3
results.quote: INFORM repeats the DAC7 pattern, so **the decision to launch in-platform payments is also a regulatory decision**, outside the EU as well as inside it: under the US INFORM Consumers Act, only sales made through the marketplace with payment processed by it count toward the high-volume seller threshold.
results.finding: The conclusion comes before its reason inside one long sentence. Flow reader A: 'The conclusion comes before its reason inside one long sentence. It is a minor re-read.'
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 13 ('The INFORM paragraph puts the conclusion before its reason, so I had to re-read it')

results.quote: That is **The Copy-Paste Country**, and it makes the next change cost eight times as much, once per country.
results.finding: The chapter never says Veldmark operates in eight countries, so 'eight' lands without a referent. Flow reader A: 'The chapter never says Veldmark has eight countries, so "eight" lands without a referent.'
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 14 ('The chapter never says Veldmark has eight countries, so the number came without grounding')

results.quote: Across the group and across every rule in this chapter, not only the listing fields of Vertical Rules, verticals weigh the same laws differently, differ most in listing rules, and enter DAC7 only when the platform handles the money.
results.finding: Both readers mark the section's position 'unclear': a cross-cutting summary by vertical placed between Trade-offs and Failure Modes interrupts the evaluative run, and both propose moving it after Beyond the EU or folding it into Vertical Rules. The difficulty comes from the spec's order (verticals grouped with the judging sections by the book's template), not from the prose.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, section 2 and section 4 (Vertical Differences 'Unclear ... it interrupts the evaluative run'; same reordering proposed)

results.quote: Across the group and across every rule in this chapter, not only the listing fields of Vertical Rules, verticals weigh the same laws differently, differ most in listing rules, and enter DAC7 only when the platform handles the money.
results.finding: The opening sentence itself is hard to parse (three predicates after a stacked qualifier). Flow reader A: 'This is a hard sentence to parse.' Separate from the section's position: even in place, the sentence can be split.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 15 ('The opening sentence of Vertical Differences was the hardest in the chapter ... I read it twice before it parsed')

Every term on does_not_know is given before or at first use: legal roles in the Concepts table, statement of reasons glossed in the scene, the Transparency Database in the DSA section, obligation/control/evidence and compliance by design in Concepts, P2B/UCPD/CRD/Omnibus in Concepts ¶3 and the disclosure table, DAC7 consideration and excluded sellers in the DAC7 definitions, EPBD/DPE/Pkw-EnVKV in Vertical Rules, INFORM glossed in GDPR ¶3. Femke, the Essen Golf and the Lyon apartment are on already_knows (their reintroduction is recorded under flow_is_followable).

The introduction opens with a direct statement of a change (end-of-project legal review no longer works) backed by concrete obligations; none of placeholder, restated question, dictionary, 'dawn of man' or book report.
From Trust to Money opens with a Part V synthesis, applies it to one decision and ends on a course of action and hand-off; no 'in conclusion' opener, no new subtopic, not a rephrased thesis alone.

¶1 states what no single chapter states (Part V's four chapters produce and read the same few records; trust is one platform because its records are shared); ¶3 says why it matters (Part VI's messaging, payments, labels and billing step onto it; four stacks pay again).

¶2 returns to the Part V introduction's test (who, which policy version, where it propagated, how to prove it a year later) for the 7 March 2027 suspension and to Ingrid's reproducibility question from the scene. Reader A found the test's source outside the chapter, but the draft restates it in full, as the callback requires.

The cold reader predicted the scene (irreproducible 2026 report), legal roles, DSA, ranking/consumer transparency, GDPR, DAC7, property and vehicle rules, UK/US, the five components, trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes, CA view, questions and Part V's close, in roadmap order; evidence as legal texts, the Transparency Database and fictional Veldmark; scope EU-first, not legal advice; claim of a few shared artifacts. Matches AC-2 expected.

The cold reader names one shared decision record feeding statements, the Transparency Database and reports; every reported number as a saved, versioned query over immutable events; the obligation register linking obligation, control and evidence query; payments as a perimeter change into DAC7 (reporting platform operator) and trader traceability, a regulatory decision before design is final; DAC7 aggregation from the payment ledger, early flagging near the threshold, and a separate tax profile. Matches AC-1 expected.

From Trust to Money ¶1 states the Part V synthesis (four chapters produce and read the same few records: decision record, risk scores and clusters, identity claims and trader record, the law's five components); ¶3 gives the Part VI so-what (messaging, payments into DAC7 and the legal perimeter, labels on paid placements, trader records feeding billing; four stacks pay again); ¶2 returns explicitly to the Part V test for one decision. Matches AC-4 expected.
